Document Analysis and Organizational Synthesis
Steelmaking scheduling energy efficiency and intelligent automation
Jonathan Elbaum
Task 1 Inventory and Initial Scan
The archive contains 31 papers spanning operational research, industrial AI and human-centered 
deployment. The inventory below records the requested title, complete author list, venue, publication date, 
author keywords and an initial abstract-level snippet for every document.
Automated extraction and verification method
 The ZIP archive was enumerated to establish the document count and filenames.
 PDF metadata and the first three pages of every file were extracted automatically.
 Title, author, venue, date and keyword fields were parsed from the article front matter.
 Each result was checked against the visible first page because several PDFs had blank or incorrect 
embedded metadata.
 Initial snippets were condensed from each abstract to provide a comparable first-pass description.

Complexity and tools brought to the problem
The domain is difficult because steel processes are tightly coupled, energy intensive and constrained by 
temperature, residence time, product sequence, capacity, equipment condition and safety. Uncertain 
arrivals, processing times, prices and failures make static schedules fragile. The document set therefore 
brings together optimization for explicit constraints, forecasting for uncertain inputs, simulation and digital 
twins for executable plant state, DRL for repeated adaptive decisions, and XAI plus human oversight for 
accountable use.

Initial scan findings
 The strongest evidence concerns energy-aware and uncertainty-aware scheduling.
 Digital-twin papers connect optimization with live operational state, while DRL papers address adaptive 
decision speed.
 Explainability and human-factor papers are fewer and are rarely validated with steel-plant operators.
 Most studies demonstrate technical feasibility in simulations or bounded industrial cases; the set 
provides limited long-term evidence on governance, cybersecurity, model drift and workforce adoption.

Task 2 Topographical Mapping
The map uses two complementary structures. The hierarchy defines the domain from problem to method 
and governance. The cross-reference network links individual papers that share processes, methods or 
implementation dependencies.
Hierarchical topic tree
Figure 1. The domain separates physical decisions, decision methods and deployment requirements. 
These branches converge in a deployable scheduling capability.

Paper-to-paper cross-reference network
Figure 2. Nodes are paper numbers from Task 1. Pale links connect papers within the same cluster; darker 
links mark important cross-cluster relationships.

Link Reason

tardiness scheduling trade-off.

disruption or uncertainty.

release or gas-flow conditions.

Knowledge concentrations and isolated areas
 Concentration: furnace energy scheduling, multi-objective trade-offs and uncertainty handling.
 Bridge: digital twins link sensors and operational state to optimization and DRL.
 Isolation: XAI papers connect weakly to steel-specific case evidence.
 Gap: few papers treat quality, maintenance, energy, safety and emissions in one plant-wide model.
 Gap: cybersecurity, accountability, model ownership, drift monitoring and long-term operator adoption 
receive little empirical attention.

Mandatory trade-offs for management
 Nominal energy efficiency versus resilience to uncertainty.
 Global optimization quality versus computation time and operational responsiveness.
 Adaptive learning performance versus verification and auditability.
 Frequent rescheduling versus schedule stability for operators and downstream teams.
 Autonomous action versus human accountability in safety- and quality-relevant situations.

Operating workflow
 Ingest and validate current plant and energy-market state.
 Update forecasts and uncertainty ranges.
 Generate a robust feasible baseline with explicit hard constraints.
 Use the adaptive policy only for decision classes that passed simulation and stress testing.
 Present the recommended schedule with objective changes, uncertainty, binding constraints and a 
counterfactual alternative.
 Execute automatically only within the approved low-risk envelope; escalate other cases.
 Record outcomes, overrides and reasons for monitoring and retraining.

Measures and controls
 Primary outcomes: energy per tonne, energy cost, peak demand, tardiness, throughput and schedule 
stability.
 Guardrails: temperature, residence time, product quality, capacity, maintenance windows and safety 
constraints.
 Governance: named operational and model owners, role-based access, audit logs, drift checks, fallback 
schedules and rollback.
 Adoption: explanation usefulness, override rate, override reasons and response time.

Task 5 Final Report and Strategic Storytelling
Executive recommendation
Approve a staged pilot at one reheating-furnace and rolling interface. Build a reliable live state and robust 
optimization baseline first. Introduce DRL only after the twin, constraints and fallback have been validated. 
Require an explanation and accountable authority for every high-impact recommendation.
Attention
Energy is consumed while furnaces heat product and while equipment waits. Delays, uncertain arrivals, 
breakdowns and poor coordination can increase both energy use and tardiness. Papers 1, 7, 12, 22 and 27 
show that scheduling itself is an energy lever, while papers 2, 3, 24 and 28 show why a nominally efficient 
schedule can fail under uncertainty.
Interest
The evidence provides a practical combination. Digital twins supply a current and testable plant state (10, 
19, 26, 30). Robust multi-objective optimization protects feasibility and exposes trade-offs (3, 12, 17, 22, 
28). DRL can accelerate repeated decisions and respond to energy conditions after safe training (5, 9, 20, 
21). XAI and counterfactuals show why the schedule changed and what alternative is possible (4, 6, 8, 13).
Desire
The organization gains a scheduling capability rather than a single opaque model. Management can see 
energy, delivery and stability effects together. Operators receive recommendations grounded in current 
plant state, with binding constraints and alternatives. Risk remains controlled through hard metallurgical 
limits, approval tiers, fallback schedules and audit logs, consistent with the human-centered and safety 
arguments in papers 16 and 25.
Action
 Authorize an eight-week baseline and data-readiness phase.
 Select one furnace-rolling interface and appoint an operational owner, model owner and safety 
approver.
 Agree the hard constraint catalogue and five headline KPIs before model development.
 Build the scoped twin and run robust recommendations in shadow mode.
 Move to controlled execution only after performance, safety, stability and explanation gates are passed.
 Evaluate restricted DRL only after the deterministic and robust baseline is operating reliably.

Evidence limitations
The document set supports technical feasibility, but it does not justify a universal savings promise. Several 
papers use simulations or bounded industrial cases, methods optimize different objectives, and long-term 
adoption evidence is limited. The proposed gates therefore require measured site results before expansion.
